items.title: Unleashing AI for preclinical drug development
items.abstract_or_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping preclinical drug development across target discovery, therapeutic design, synthesis, functional characterization and safety assessment. In this review, we present an integrated view of AI across the preclinical pipeline, beginning with target identification, modality selection and representation learning for molecular, protein, structural, cellular and multimodal data. We then examine major generative modeling paradigms including autoregressive, latent-variable, diffusion, flow-based and guided approaches and their applications across small molecules, peptides, enzymes, antibodies, Tcell receptors and mRNA therapeutics. We discuss how these methods support de novo design, structure- and pocket-conditioned generation, sequence–structure co-design, affinity and activity optimization, developability engineering and synthesis-aware discovery. We further review AI-enabled retrosynthesis, reaction prediction and closed-loop experimental optimization, emphasizing the distinction between computational synthesizability and experimentally executable chemistry. Beyond molecular generation, we organize functional prediction from binding and kinetics through target engagement, pharmacological activity, mechanism of action, pathway response and phenotypic outcome. We also examine singlecell perturbation modeling, organoid-based drug-response prediction, toxicity and off-target assessment, and prospective validation across therapeutic modalities. Across these areas, we highlight the importance of uncertainty estimation, out-of-distribution generalization, reproducibility and experimentally grounded benchmarking. Finally, we discuss how integrating generative AI, mechanistic biology and iterative design–make–test–analyze cycles could transform AI from isolated predictive tools into decision-support systems for preclinical drug development.

items.title: CP-GFM-SGX: Topology-Aware Cyclic Peptide Generation and Design with Receptor-Conditioned Structural Evaluation and Experimental KRAS Affinity Optimization
items.abstract_or_text: Cyclic-peptide discovery requires molecular topology, atomic structure, receptor-associated evidence and computational decisions to remain consistent across a multistage workflow. We present CP-GFM-SGX, an all-atom generative AI model for cyclic-peptide design that integrates a topology-aware generative core with a Unified Evidence State Machine (UESM) to track candidate identity, chemical validity, provenance, typed failures and bounded computation. We evaluated three distinct aspects of the system. In Track A, a frozen five-complex known-ligand benchmark with 100 scheduled poses per complex, the native-free FULL route selected a ligand-backbone pose with root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) below 2 Å in four of five systems; retrospective best-of-100 evaluation found a sub-2-Å pose in all five (median selected RMSD, 1.72 Å). In Track B, matched true-pocket versus shuffled-pocket comparisons favored the specified pocket in all seven main targets (median of target medians, +172.6 Rosetta energy units; weakest margin, +3.9 for MCL-1–9CDT). An exploratory post-protocol assessor admitted 42/42, 42/42 and 40/42 selected top-K slots in the full, condition-masked and post hoc head-to-tail arms, respectively. In Track C, FULL UESM produced the specified protective outcomes for six deterministic synthetic fault fixtures and one additional missing-evidence case; targeted ablations isolated the roles of provenance and failure propagation. In a separate KRAS G12D–GDP experimental-feedback series, synthesis and SPR/BLI testing of cyclic-peptide analogues guided position-2 basic-side-chain selection and dual-basic-group placement, advancing the reported SPR affinity from approximately 60 µM for CRO-748 to approximately 6 µM for 748-R1 and approximately 1 µM for 748-RK. Comparisons using the 31-dimension Structured Capability and Evidence Grid (SCEG-31D) demonstrate that CP-GFM-SGX exhibits certain superiority over other design platforms in multiple aspects. Together, we evaluate a topology-aware generative artificial intelligence workflow for receptor-focused cyclic-peptide design and show, in a KRAS feedback series, how binding measurements guide iterative chemical optimization.

items.title: Drug Molecular and Route Similarity-Aware Retrieval-Augmented LLM Generation with Knowledge Graph for Semantic Reasoning
items.abstract_or_text: To address the inherent limitations of large language models (LLMs) in chemical synthesis—hallucinations, and low knowledge dense—this study presents a Knowledge Graph–enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework (KG-RAG-LLM) with a multi-scale calculation of molecular and route similarity. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that KG-RAG-LLM significantly mitigates hallucinations, increasing the proportion of concrete chemical information in generated responses to 39.52%–40.87%, drastically outperforming baseline LLMs and standard literature-based RAG pipelines in response completeness and accuracy. To overcome the inability of traditional 2D linear fingerprints to capture 3D spatial properties and reaction path variations, we further developed a multidimensional molecular and route similarity calculation combining SimHash, core similarity, and FCFP, as an alternative to Route CGR representations coupled with UMAP dimensionality reduction. This formulation accurately distinguishes between subtle and distinct synthetic strategies, demonstrating superior precision over traditional clustering methods for fuzzy retrieval of synthetic routes. Overall, this work provides a reliable, knowledge-dense solution for intelligent retrosynthetic Semantic Reasoning.

items.title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

items.title: AI-guided discovery for low-resource peptide engineering using evolutionary scale modeling
items.abstract_or_text: Data scarcity is a major bottleneck in artificial intelligence (AI)-guided peptide engineering, where experimental training sets often contain only tens to a few hundred sequences, and it is difficult to judge in advance whether a protein language model (PLM) will effectively guide iterative discovery before committing to wet-lab work. Here we present SCARSE, a machine learning framework that couples ESM2 protein language model embeddings with Gaussian process regression. Benchmarked across 24 diverse peptide and small-protein datasets spanning substitution and indel variants, antimicrobial peptides, and hemolytic peptides, SCARSE significantly outperformed hand-engineered descriptor baselines on substitution and indel tasks in low-data regimes (20-500 training samples) and performed comparably on short non-mutant peptides. In active learning simulations it consistently prioritized high-performing candidates, discovering up to 7-fold more top-tier peptides than random sampling. Cross-validation (CV) R2 correlated strongly with final active learning performance (Pearson r = 0.80-0.84), and evaluating on as few as 50 labeled peptides reduced CV R2 variance enough for it to serve as a practical, data-efficient criterion for assessing model suitability before iterative screening. SCARSE thus provides an early diagnostic indicator for active learning success and is freely available as an open-source Python package (pip) and through an interactive Hugging Face Spaces web interface.

items.title: From Vacuum Geometry to Solution-Phase Electronic Properties and Thermodynamics via Equivariant Neural Networks
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce a general framework for predicting solution-phase quantum-mechanical (QM) properties of drug-like molecules directly from gas-phase geometries, without solvent-specific structural optimization or property calculations. Using current equivariant neural network (ENN) architectures, such as MACE and Allegro, we demonstrate that they can also predict extensive and intensive QM properties in implicit water at a high level of theory. Direct-and ∆-learning strategies are employed for this prediction task using the Aquamarine dataset, which provides QM properties for the same molecules in both environments. The developed models are systematically evaluated for scalability to larger molecules, transferability across chemical space, and generalization to out-of-equilibrium configurations. Our results show that, despite substantial differences between gas-and solution-phase conformational ensembles, the models can accurately reconstruct ensemble-averaged solution-phase properties from gas-phase molecular dynamics. We further integrate the learned QM properties into the QUEDsol framework (“QUantum Electronic Descriptors in SOLution”) as electronic descriptors for hydration free-energy prediction. A simple and interpretable quadratic regression model trained on the FreeSolv dataset achieves state-of-the-art performance on the challenging and chemically diverse FlexiSol benchmark, outperforming previously reported QM-and ML-based approaches. These results establish ENNs as a versatile approach for inter-phase molecular property prediction and demonstrate that environment-specific QM descriptors generated from gas-phase geometries can provide transferable inputs for complex thermodynamic modeling.

items.title: Modular Cell-Free Extract Mixing Enables Soluble, Active Biomanufacturing of Difficult-to-Express and Aggregation-Prone Proteins
items.abstract_or_text: Cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) is a powerful platform for rapid protein prototyping and biomanufacturing, but expression of complex proteins remains limited by labor-intensive extract preparation as well as the inability of conventional Escherichia coli extracts to efficiently support disulfide bond formation and prevent protein aggregation. We previously developed a Cell-Free Autoinduction (CFAI) workflow that simplifies extract preparation, however, CFAI-derived extracts retain the folding limitations of standard E. coli systems for producing traditionally difficult proteins. Here, we address these challenges by utilizing extracts enriched with molecular chaperones or Erv1p-based oxidative folding catalysts and combining them through a modular extract mixing strategy to enable independent tuning of the cell-free folding environment. This workflow supplies folding factors through enriched extracts, avoiding recurring purchases of purified supplements and enabling a modeled reagent-cost advantage. To evaluate real-world applications and utility of lysate mixing for protein production, we demonstrate a 10-fold increase in solubility of the aggregation-prone bacterial toxin Colicin M, achieving >95% soluble protein while retaining antimicrobial activity. We further used a Design of Experiments (DoE) framework to optimize combinations of chaperone-enriched and Erv1p-based oxidative folding extracts containing either protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) or DsbC. The optimized compositions produced >95% soluble truncated human tissue plasminogen activator (vtPA), comprising the kringle 2 and protease domains, while preserving enzymatic activity. Together, these results demonstrate that CFAI-derived modular extract mixing provides a tunable, high-throughput strategy with low modeled materials costs for tailoring cell-free biochemical environments for difficult-to-express proteins, expanding CFPS utility for protein engineering and biomanufacturing.

items.title: Beyond the Final Layer: Evaluating Single-Cell Foundation Model Representations for Molecular Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are commonly benchmarked using final-layer embeddings, although useful depth may depend on the task. We evaluate Geneformer, scBERT, scGPT, and scFoundation as frozen feature extractors for cell-type and perturbation-response prediction using layer-wise probes, leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) selection, readout controls, representation diagnostics, centered kernel alignment (CKA), and retrieval/collapse analyses. Intermediate layers significantly improve cell-type accuracy for scGPT and scBERT in several settings, while Geneformer and scFoundation generally show performance comparable to their final layers. For perturbation prediction, LODO identifies layer 1 as an earliest-on-par candidate across all four models, without establishing universal superiority. Paired scGPT CLS and mean-pooling analyses show that readout affects preferred depth. CKA and representation metrics reveal model- and task-dependent geometric changes, while retrieval and collapse checks support the robustness of perturbation findings. We recommend reporting extraction depth, readout, selection protocol, and task-specific diagnostics. A validated non-final layer may also reduce computation, although efficiency was not directly benchmarked.

items.title: Probing Physical Intuition in Large Language Models through Partner-Dependent Mutation Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Structure-guided mutation design requires relating a proposed substitution to its molecular environment to anticipate its effects. Existing evaluations of large language models (LLMs) in protein engineering emphasize sequence-based prediction or tool-integrated workflows, leaving unclear whether LLMs themselves can infer mutation effects from structural evidence without dedicated predictors. We evaluate physical intuition-qualitative reasoning that connects structural observations with molecular interaction principles-using a benchmark that tests the same substitution in the same protein across different binding partners, with predictions based on local atomic coordinates and no dedicated mutation-effect predictors. In the tested comparisons, the best-performing LLM achieved group accuracy comparable to the evaluated energy predictors and Biomni, an LLM-driven tool workflow, while the methods differed in their prediction patterns. Most evaluated LLMs achieved higher group accuracy for larger affinity improvements. Structural interventions support selective dependence on mutation-site and partner information, while assessable structural claims largely agree with the supplied coordinates. These findings support direct LLM structural reasoning as a basis for developing rational mutation-design tools that connect molecular observations with partner-specific effects.

items.title: Reformulating Protein Corona Prediction as Universal Protein-conditioned Learning
items.abstract_or_text: When nanoparticles enter biological environments, their surfaces are rapidly coated by proteins, forming a protein corona that governs their biological identity and downstream responses. Existing computational methods treat each protein as an independent prediction task, preventing the learning of shared adsorption principles and limiting generalization beyond experimentally characterized proteins. Here we introduce NanoPCT, a universal protein-conditioned learning framework that jointly models nanoparticle physicochemical properties and protein sequence representations. Using frozen ESM-2 embeddings and a joint interaction transformer, NanoPCT learns transferable representations of nano-bio interaction patterns across hundreds of proteins and maintains robust performance as protein diversity increases. The learned protein representation further enables zero-shot prediction for previously unseen proteins and biologically distinct protein groups through classifier reconstruction in embedding space. Beyond prediction, NanoPCT supports large-scale in silico inverse design and reveals consistent adsorption preferences between observed and unseen protein populations, suggesting that it captures transferable interaction patterns rather than protein-specific memorization. NanoPCT provides a unified framework for protein corona prediction, zero-shot generalization, and rational nanomaterial design.

items.title: FMS2Lib: A Machine Learning-Ready Tandem Mass Spectral Library for Nontargeted Analysis of Non-conventional PFAS
items.abstract_or_text: Nontargeted identification of non-conventional per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), including fluorinated pharmaceuticals and pesticides, remains challenging. Existing machine learning models for nontargeted analysis, primarily trained on tandem mass spectra of nonfluorinated compounds, may not generalize well to non-conventional PFAS because of their distinct mass spectrometric chemistry. Here, we established FMS2Lib, an experimental tandem mass spectral library containing 34,686 fluorinated drug-like compounds (F 1-4 ), to support machine learning-based nontargeted PFAS analysis. We demonstrated that training with FMS2Lib substantially improved the performance of existing models for both molecular formula prediction and structure annotation. We further applied these models to identify PFAS in passive samplers from wastewater effluents and surface waters and in high-throughput laboratory biotransformation experiments, revealing dozens of non-conventional PFAS and their biotransformation products. Collectively, FMS2Lib addresses a major data bottleneck in machine learning-based nontargeted analysis of non-conventional PFAS.

items.title: Building the Data Foundations for the Design and Discovery of Transition Metal Complexes
items.abstract_or_text: The unique chemistry of transition metal complexes (TMCs) enables several advanced technologies in diverse fields including renewable energies, medicine, and catalysis. Machine learning methods can accelerate their rational design but are bounded by limited dataset sizes, restricted chemical scopes, and insufficient quality. This Perspective surveys the current landscape of TMC datasets and investigates how they seek to address these challenges. The analysis focuses on the data curation processes as well as the scope of the properties provided, and their level of theory. Furthermore, the applications and methodological advancements enabled by TMC datasets are reviewed, including the generative design of metal ligands and the evolutionary optimization of TMCs. The Perspective concludes by outlining future directions, with particular emphasis on extending data to broader chemical scopes including non-equilibrium geometries, establishing community-wide data formats and benchmarks, and developing strategies to effectively integrate heterogeneous data sources.

items.title: CHORUS: A proteome-scale atlas of membrane interaction interfaces constructed using cross-protein language model embeddings from sequences alone
items.abstract_or_text: Membrane proteins drive vital cellular signaling and bioenergetics yet resolving their physical interaction interfaces remains hindered by the paucity of experimental complexes and the breakdown of sequence alignments across hydrophobic bilayers. Here, we present CHORUS, a sequence-only deep-learning framework that decodes interaction sites across membrane proteins without requiring 3D structures, multiple sequence alignments (MSAs), or predefined partner identities. By systematically synthesizing complementary latent representations across diverse protein language model (pLM) families and functional layer depths, CHORUS outperforms 18 established sequence- and structure-based methods across 4,655 homology-isolated test contexts (average precision: 0.643), demonstrating amplified predictive capacity within the lipid-embedded core (0.746). We show that CHORUS delineates quaternary contact boundaries across megadalton respiratory supercomplexes directly from sequences alone (0.984). We deliver the CHORUS Atlas (https://chorus.atlas.sunnylab.org), providing precomputed, residue-resolved interaction landscapes for 80,619 reviewed transmembrane proteins spanning 4,918 species and 33.7 million residues to empower interactome-scale discovery and allosteric therapeutic design.

items.title: CAN it work? Using hydroxyethyl acrylate or methacrylate to turn epoxy-amine thermosets into covalent adaptable network materials.
items.abstract_or_text: Epoxy-amine thermosets can be converted into covalent adaptable networks (CANs) by adding β-aminoester-based curing agents to the formulation. This is achieved by utilizing commercially available di- or trifunctional acrylate monomers, which react with the amine component via an aza-Michael addition. Consequently, this approach is inherently scalable and holds high industrial relevance. In this study, the fundamental applicability of two commodity chemicals—namely 2-hydroxyethyl acrylate (HEA) and 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA)—for this purpose is investigated, aiming to provide an additional handle to mitigate the rapid viscosity increase of the formulations. Using a model epoxy resin consisting of bisphenol A diglycidyl ether (DGEBA) and 1,3-bis(aminomethyl)cyclohexane (BAC), it was demonstrated that a Lewis-base catalyst (1-methylimidazole) is necessary to incorporate the hydroxy groups of HEA and HEMA into the network. Contrary to expectations, this incorporation proceeds predominantly through a condensation reaction that liberates ethylene glycol. Finally, a formulation consisting of 1 equiv. DGEBA, 0.5 equiv. BAC, 1 equiv. HEA, and 0.025 equiv. 1-methylimidazole was found to offer a good compromise, providing both satisfactory reprocessability and a sufficiently high glass transition temperature (74 °C). Compared to a reference formulation made with a trifunctional acrylate monomer, the CAN made with HEA is characterized by a lower glass transition temperature, a similar flow activation energy, a lower storage modulus, and distinctly longer relaxation times. Both acrylate-based CAN materials aged under thermal stress, which resulted in higher storage moduli and glass transition temperatures upon reprocessing. A protocol for characterizing such modulus changes under thermal stress is suggested, consisting of performing repeated frequency sweeps for at least 1 h at temperatures slightly exceeding the maximum temperature of the stress relaxation measurements.

items.title: Inherent limitations of zero-shot mutation prediction in protein engineering
items.abstract_or_text: Predicting mutation effects is critical for protein engineering. A commonly pursued strategy is zero-shot prediction with deep-learning models, whose performance is typically evaluated using aggregate benchmark scores that obscure multidimensional biological tradeoffs. Here, we evaluate sequence, structure, and hybrid foundation models across curated datasets to expose the practical limitations of zero-shot predictions. We demonstrate that model performance is highly variable and heavily influenced by experimental noise and competing phenotypic goals. Notably, predictions from competing models often correlate more strongly with one another than with experimental outcomes. While current models effectively filter deleterious mutations and enrich high-scoring variants for natural functions, they struggle to identify precise optimal mutations and consistently fail to predict mutations that drive new-to-nature functions. These models learn from evolutionary constraints that tend to oppose the extreme biophysical optimizations required in targeted engineering. Consequently, zero-shot scoring serves as a valuable initial filter but cannot substitute for task-specific prediction.

items.title: Sequence context decodes multi-state conformational heterogeneity from crystallographic B-factors
items.abstract_or_text: Protein function is governed by conformational ensembles, yet the overwhelming majority of experimentally determined structures capture only static snapshots, leaving the multi-state heterogeneity that underlies biological activity largely inaccessible. X-ray crystallography, the dominant source of these structures, does carry one experimental proxy for motion, the atomic B-factor, but crystal packing and refinement artifacts frequently obscure its link to solution-state dynamics. Here we show that sequence context is sufficient to decode a protein's multi-state conformational heterogeneity from this seemingly noisy signal. We introduce the B-Factor Corrector (BFC), a fine-tuned protein language model that reframes B-factor analysis from a purely physical calculation into a sequence-context-aware translation task. By leveraging deep contextual embeddings to decouple intrinsic conformational heterogeneity from lattice constraints, BFC recovers the residue-wise heterogeneity ranking derived from crystallographic structural ensembles, reproducing the normalized profile at a Pearson correlation of 0.83 while correcting the distortions that analytical formulas leave in the raw signal. We further demonstrate the utility of this sequence-inferred signal across structural-biology applications: it provides an integrable prior for molecular docking that is statistically equivalent to experimental B-factors, unmasks cryptic conformational heterogeneity essential for chaperone function, and guides the energetic refinement of antibody interfaces to resolve steric conflicts. These results suggest that the static structures of the Protein Data Bank can be effectively repurposed to decode the conformational heterogeneity latent within them.

items.title: Targeting Lysosomal MCOLN1/TRPML1 Ion Channels to Alleviate Diabetes Mellitus via a Ca2+- CaMKKβ-AMPK pathway
items.abstract_or_text: Type 2 Diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a metabolic syndrome characterized by hyperglycemia and various complications. Current drugs are limited by side effects and resistance, necessitating novel targets and therapies. Previous studies have shown that MK-83, a synthetic agonist of transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1/ MCOLN1), a lysosomal Ca2+ channel, activates adenosine 5'-monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a key therapeutic target in diabetes. However, whether targeting TRPML1 can treat T2DM remains unclear. In this study, we found that transgenic overexpression or pharmacological activation of TRPML1 regulates AMPK phosphorylation via a Ca2+-CaMKK{beta}-dependent mechanism. This activation promotes glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) translocation and increases intracellular glucose uptake. Conversely, genetic inactivation or pharmacologically inhibition of TRPML1 blocks both AMPK activation and glucose uptake. More importantly, pharmacological activation of TRPML1 in vivo alleviates hyperglycemia in db/db mice (a T2DM model), as evidenced by random blood glucose levels, fasting blood glucose levels and HbA1c levels. Furthermore, other hallmark features of db/db mice- including impaired oral glucose tolerance, reduced insulin tolerance, and elevated ALT and AST levels- were all ameliorated upon TRPML1 activation. Hence, targeting lysosomal TRPML1 channel represents a promising therapeutic strategy for T2DM, with highly specific TRPML1 agonists as potential anti-diabetic agents.

items.title: tRNAZAP: Deep learning toolkit for nanopore tRNA signal analysis
items.abstract_or_text: tRNA are short, ~76 nucleotide-long, modification-rich molecules that play an important role in protein translation. Nanopore sequencing is the only platform capable of directly sequencing full-length, native tRNA molecules. This capability is enabled by splinted ligation of tRNA-specific adapters. As a result, the measured ionic current signal reflects a composition of both adapter and tRNA sequence features. Despite these advantages, analysis of nanopore tRNA sequencing data poses distinct computational challenges. Existing ionic current-based signal-to-sequence decoding (basecalling) models are optimized for mRNA and perform suboptimally on short, modification-dense RNA such as tRNA. Furthermore, alignment algorithms for reference-guided analysis of short-length reads are not optimized for nanopore reads with lower accuracy than Next-generation sequencing reads. To overcome these limitations, domain-specific computational approaches are required. We present tRNAZAP, a nanopore ionic current signal analysis toolkit designed to enable precise reference-guided sequence alignment. tRNAZAP operates directly on raw ionic current signals and decomposes the analysis into two complementary tasks: 1) segmentation of adapter and tRNA regions, and 2) tRNA classification, both implemented using transformer-based models. The segmentation component isolates the tRNA signal portion and extracts the corresponding nucleotide sequence as the alignment query, while the classification component identifies the tRNA type as the alignment reference without requiring sequence-level information. Together, these outputs allow direct optimal pairwise alignment between the tRNA subsequence of the full query and reference sequences. Trained on in vitro transcribed RNA data and evaluated on yeast tRNA, these models achieved ~98% classification accuracy and intersection-over-union of ~0.98 for segmentation.

items.title: High-throughput variant libraries and machine learning enable robust target-site selection for toehold-switch design in Detectrons
items.abstract_or_text: Programmable RNA sensors enable sequence-specific detection of RNA inputs for diagnostics, genetic circuit control, and multiplexed molecular readouts. Although readily programmable, their performance varies substantially with the target site selected within a transcript, making target-site selection a major challenge. Here, we report DeSTAR (Detectron Sensor TARget-site ranker), a machine-learning-assisted target-site ranking model for programmable RNA sensors. To train this model, we generated transcript-wide, single-nucleotide-resolution tiling sensor libraries across six diverse RNA targets, enabling generalization to be tested across transcripts rather than within a single RNA. In leave-one-transcript-out evaluation, DeSTAR's top-ranked sites were enriched for high-performing sensors in held-out transcripts, driven predominantly by interpretable sequence grammar in the sensor stem rather than transcript-specific patterns. Prospectively, on an unseen SARS-CoV-2 transcript, the model's top-ranked sites yielded working sensors roughly five-fold more often than random selection. These results support DeSTAR as a generalizable strategy for target-site selection in RNA sensors across transcripts.

items.title: Lipid diffusion enhanced by molecular motors
items.abstract_or_text: An experimental study of myosin I motors on a supported lipid membrane with a nematic actin filament layer is presented. The activities of myosin I motors re-organize the actin layer, in particular the morphology of +1/2 nematic defects. Data from single-particle tracking (SPT) of lipid molecules reveal two interesting features. First, the distribution of average lipid speed over a track shows two groups of lipids (high-speed and low-speed), and the proportion of lipids to be high-speed is higher in regions rich in actin. Second, by classifying short-time movement of the lipids into normal diffusion, directed motion, confined motion, and subdiffusion states, we found that lipids in regions rich in actin have a lower probability to stay in the confined and subdiffusion states and more likely to perform normal diffusion. Furthermore, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) measurements show that the diffusion of lipids in the actin-rich regions is enhanced. The SPT and FRAP results suggest that myosin I motor activities turn low-speed lipids to high-speed ones, and affect the lipid moving state by reducing confined and subdiffusive motion. As a result, lipid diffusion is enhanced by motor activities.

items.title: Mechanistic Classification of Multicatalysis
items.abstract_or_text: Multicatalysis combines two or more catalytic functions within a single reaction network and can unlock reactivity, selectivity, and synthetic efficiency that are difficult to achieve with an individual catalyst. Its mechanistic description, however, remains fragmented across partially overlapping terms such as tandem, relay, cooperative, synergistic, double-activation, and bifunctional catalysis, among others. Here, we propose a mechanism-first classification based on the relationship between catalytic functions and, specifically, on the catalytic ‘currency’ exchanged between them. When the currency is substrate-derived, the coupling is classified as tandem, cooperative, or double activation. When the exchanged currency controls catalyst state rather than contributing to the substrate framework (e.g. electrons, cofactors), the relationship is gated or regenerative, distinguished by whether activation is required only once or repeatedly during turnover. Importantly, the classification is additive, so complex reaction networks are represented as combinations of pairwise relationships. Representative reactions illustrate how this framework resolves mechanistic distinctions that are hidden by conventional labels. By linking nomenclature to the elementary connection between catalytic functions, the classification provides a compact language for comparing multicatalytic systems and a basis for more deliberate catalyst and reaction-network design.

items.title: NEVPT2 Multiple Spawning Molecular Dynamics Simulations for Uracil
items.abstract_or_text: The quasidegenerate n-electron valence state second-order perturbation theory (QD-NEVPT2) for complete active space reference wavefunctions has been implemented in the OpenMolcas package. The implementation utilizes the efficient formulation of Kollmar et al. for the electronic energy, which is extended here to the calculation of analytic derivatives. To demonstrate its utility, the method is applied to classical and non-adiabatic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of uracil. The non-adiabatic MD simulations describe the ultrafast deactivation of the initially excited bright ππ∗ state through the S 2 /S 1 conical intersection, demonstrating the applicability of the method to photochemical processes. Furthermore, a machine learning-based analysis of the trajectory data extracts key geometrical parameters that are associated with the magnitude of the time-derivative coupling.

items.title: Photochemical Aminomethylation of C(sp 3 )–H Bonds via Hydrogen Atom Transfer
items.abstract_or_text: Direct installation of an aminomethyl group onto aliphatic C–H bonds provides an attractive route to valuable amine-containing building blocks but remains challenging with conventional polar approaches. Here, we report a photochemical aminomethylation of C(sp3)–H bonds enabled by hydrogen atom transfer (HAT). Photoexcited benzophenone directly abstracts hydrogen from αamino, α-oxy, and α-thio C–H bonds, generating carbon-centered radicals that are intercepted by an in situ-formed N-protected formimine. This strategy provides direct access to protected vicinal diamines, amino alcohol derivatives, and related aminomethylated products without requiring prefunctionalization of the C–H donor. Notably, the C–H substrate can be employed as the limiting reagent, while selective radical generation suppresses overfunctionalization. Translation to continuous flow reduces reaction times from 20 h to 3 h, while improving yields for the investigated substrates, and enables scalable synthesis. Subsequent deprotection and functionalization further demonstrate the synthetic utility of the resulting aminomethylated products.

items.title: Following Nature’s Lead – Pillar[n]arene Phosphates as Versatile Molecular Hosts
items.abstract_or_text: Phosphates are ubiquitous natural recognition motifs. Their charge, hydrogen bonding, variable substitution, and reversible enzymatic installation uniquely enable complex tasks in Biology. However, they are not used extensively in supramolecular systems. Herein, we combine Nature’s modulator with supramolecular rational design, creating rim-functionalised pillar[n]arene phosphates, which act as highaffinity molecular hosts. Using robust phosphoramidite chemistry, we prepared P5Max and P6Max, based on pillar[5]arene and pillar[6]arene cores in four high yielding steps. We developed a high-throughput fluorescence displacement assay enabling us to explore a biologically focused screening panel and so rapidly investigate the recognition properties of our new hosts. P5Max and P6Max bind a series of structurally diverse chemotherapies, neuromuscular blockade agents, anaesthetics and antibiotics, with P6Max proving the more general host. We used functional assays to explore P6Max’s ability to control the biological effect of different drug classes, including highly toxic chemotherapy drugs and antibiotics. The use of high-throughput assays in host-guest systems provides a simple, rapid, and scalable route to translating supramolecular interactions to functional effect.

items.title: Bovine serum albumin interaction modulates the cellular potency of the BUB1 inhibitor BAY-1816032: fluorescence, molecular docking, and mesothelioma cell evidence
items.abstract_or_text: Albumin binding can substantially alter the unbound concentration and apparent cellular potency of small-molecule anticancer agents. BAY-1816032 is a selective BUB1 kinase inhibitor with activity in malignant pleural mesothelioma, but its interaction with serum albumin has not been defined. This study combined intrinsic bovine serum albumin (BSA) fluorescence measurements, molecular docking, and cell-viability assays to examine whether albumin association influences BAY-1816032 activity. BAY-1816032 produced pronounced quenching of BSA fluorescence at low drug-to-protein molar ratios, and the quenching response was greater at mildly acidic pH than at mildly basic pH. Docking to BSA (PDB 4F5S) placed the top-ranked pose in Sudlow site I (subdomain IIA), with a Vina score of -7.8 kcal/mol and predicted hydrogen-bond contacts with Tyr149, Arg256, and Asp450. In NCI-H28, NCI-H2052, NCI-H2452, and AB12 mesothelioma cells, supplementation of 10% fetal bovine serum medium with 2% (w/v; 20 mg/mL) BSA shifted BAY-1816032 concentration-response curves to the right. Relative to 10% serum alone, IC50 values increased from 2.4 to 11.1 uM in H28, 3.6 to 22.0 uM in H2052, 2.0 to 4.9 uM in H2452, and 2.4 to 11.1 uM in AB12. These data support an albumin-dependent reduction in the freely available drug fraction and identify site I as the leading computational binding-site hypothesis. Because fluorescence-intensity and docking data do not independently establish a dissociation constant or quenching mechanism, direct unbound-fraction measurements and competitive displacement experiments are required for quantitative confirmation.

items.title: Coordinated Enhancement of Molecular and Spatial Fidelity for Biological Inference in Spatial Transcriptomics
items.abstract_or_text: Understanding tissue organization requires accurate molecular quantification and faithful spatial localization. Spatial omics, particularly spatial transcriptomics (ST), face measurement trade-offs that limit simultaneous achievement of molecular and spatial fidelity across spatial resolution, detection sensitivity, molecular-tissue alignment and cell-level fidelity. Existing computational methods typically target individual aspects and optimize them in isolation, despite their interdependence. Here we present FOCUS, a multimodal generative foundation model for coordinated ST enhancement. FOCUS integrates native ST with histology images, cell masks, scRNA-seq references and spatial co-expression priors through task-specific modules, with cross-task coordination enabling joint correction of co-occurring limitations. FOCUS improved the performance of individual enhancement tasks and provided additional gains with coordinated mitigation of coupled limitations. Across immunology, tissue development and oncology, FOCUS recovered biologically consistent patterns obscured in native ST or isolated enhancement, enabling clearer inference of neutrophil-tumor interactions, spatial osteocyte differentiation and primary-metastatic HNSCC programs. Together, FOCUS establishes coordinated enhancement of molecular and spatial fidelity as a strategy for downstream biological inference from ST.

items.title: CRISCross: Integration of Epigenetic Information for Deep-Learning-Based Prediction of CRISPR-Cas9 Off-Targets Across Cell Types
items.abstract_or_text: CRISPR-Cas9 enables precise genome editing but remains limited by off-target effects, raising safety concerns and necessitating accurate prediction. Although epigenetic features influence Cas9 binding and cleavage, their predictive signals are often weak, highlyvariable, and context-dependent, limiting the effectiveness of existing machine learning approaches. Cross-cell-type settings are especially challenging: epigenetic landscapes differ substantially, and models trained on one cell type frequently fail to generalize. Here, we systematically investigate the role of epigenetic context in off-target prediction and demonstrate that its utility depends on modeling interactions with sequence features rather than treating it as an independent signal. Tabular and deep learning experiments demonstrate that epigenetic features provide a consistent but modestly complementary signal, and that late-stage fusion strategies are insufficient to effectively exploit this information. To address this, we introduce CRISCross, a cross-attention-based architecture that captures sequence-epigenetic interactions at the nucleotide level, alongside CRISPRAT, a synthetic pretraining strategy that learns transferable representations from genome-derived sgRNA-off-target pairs without relying on dataset-specific pretraining. CRISCross, incorporating AlphaGenome-derived chromatin accessibility signals, shows better predictive performance than sequence-only baselines across three independent test datasets spanning two cell types, demonstrating improved generalization across guide RNAs, datasets, and cellular contexts. This is particularly relevant for therapeutic applications involving cell types or patient-derived contexts that lack dedicated experimental datasets. In such settings, predicted chromatin accessibility may provide scalable contextual information when direct epigenomic profiling is unavailable or impractical. Together, these results show that accurate CRISPR off-target prediction benefits from interaction-aware integration of epigenetic context alongside generalizable pretraining strategies.

items.title: Atomic-Scale Insights into the Surface Chemistry, Surface Stability, and Floatability of Spodumene and Montebrasite with Fatty Acid Collectors
items.abstract_or_text: Spodumene and montebrasite are minerals that contain significant quantities of lithium and are often found together in phosphate-rich lithium pegmatites. Separating these two minerals by flotation is key to efficient downstream lithium extraction from each. Understanding the crystal and surface properties of both minerals is an important step towards their separation by flotation. We present a systematic study of the surface properties of spodumene and montebrasite, and their interactions with fatty acid collectors, using density functional theory calculations. Our results showed that, for montebrasite, the most dominant surfaces were (110) ≈ (012̅) > (102̅) > (12̅0) > (212̅), with (110) ≈ (012̅) being the most represented (56 %). The Al-terminated (110) surface was the dominant surface on spodumene, accounting for 70 % of the crystal surface area, followed by (111̅) > (111) > (101̅) > (001), consistent with available experimental data. The Wulff equilibrium morphology showed that both minerals are elongated/prismatic, consistent with their naturally occurring crystals, but spodumene is less reactive to flotation reagents than montebrasite. Surface electronic density of states showed that Li and Al states dominate the bottom of the conduction band of spodumene (110) and montebrasite (110) and are available to hybridize with oxygen states of the COO- functional group of fatty acid collectors. Energetics calculations show that both minerals interact with fatty acid collectors via surface Al and Li, but more strongly for montebrasite than spodumene (–18.6 kcal/mol vs +11.05 kcal/mol). Therefore, montebrasite is more floatable with fatty acid collectors than spodumene, making it convenient to separate these two minerals by first recovering montebrasite to the flotation concentrate, resulting in a spodumene-enriched tailings product. Less favorable adsorption energies explain the need to activate/pretreat spodumene before flotation to overcome the energy barrier for fatty-acid adsorption, with spodumene activation by high-density conditioning performed only after montebrasite flotation. This study further demonstrates that the interaction energy of fatty acids with mineral surfaces does not depend on chain length, regardless of mineral type. Our findings open a new direction for efficient lithium production from phosphate-rich lithium pegmatites by generating a montebrasite concentrate while simultaneously upgrading the feed to the spodumene flotation circuit.

items.title: ASC specks and α-synuclein amplify microglial NLRP3 inflammasome activation and co-localize with Lewy body pathology
items.abstract_or_text: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of several chronic neurodegenerative disorders, including Parkinson's disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies, and is closely associated with microglial activation. The inflammasome adaptor protein apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a caspase activation and recruitment domain (ASC) undergoes oligomerization upon inflammasome activation, resulting in the formation of ASC specks. These structures are recognized by microglia as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), thereby promoting inflammatory signaling. Recent studies have demonstrated that extracellular ASC specks associate with amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}), and that uptake of ASC-A{beta} composites by microglia amplifies pro-inflammatory responses. Although ASC specks have also been shown to potentiate -synuclein (Syn) preformed fibril-induced pathology, their interaction with monomeric Syn and their effects on inflammasome activation remain poorly understood. Here, we co-stimulated murine SIM-A9 microglia with ASC-Syn assemblies and evaluated their effects on NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Electron microscopy revealed a close association between ASC fibrils and Syn monomers. Exposure of microglia to ASC-Syn enhanced NLRP3 inflammasome activation, as evidenced by increased ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activation, and secretion of IL-1{beta} and IL-18, when compared to ASC or Syn alone. In addition, immunohistochemical analyses of post mortem brain tissue from patients with dementia with Lewy bodies demonstrated ASC expression in regions exhibiting Syn pathology and showed ASC co-localization with Syn within Lewy bodies. Collectively, these findings identify ASC-Syn assemblies as potent amplifiers of NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and suggest a mechanism through which they may contribute to sustained neuroinflammation in synucleinopathies.

items.title: Transcriptomic reconstruction of an interregional molecular connectome in schizophrenia
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Schizophrenia is increasingly viewed as a disorder of multi-regional brain networks, but molecular and pathophysiological hypotheses are often studied at the level of single brain regions or neurotransmitter systems. A multi-regional, multi-neurotransmitter analysis is needed to clarify how molecular abnormalities relate to circuit-level hypotheses of the disorder. Methods: Transcriptomic data from 2,209 post-mortem brain samples spanning five brain regions in 1,037 individuals were integrated. Directed connectivity strengths between regions were estimated using co-expression between presynaptic and postsynaptic neurotransmission-related genes. These estimates constitute an "interregional molecular connectome". Macaque transcriptomic data were used to benchmark the estimation pipeline against reference macaque connectomes. Connectivity differences between healthy controls and patients with schizophrenia were calculated, and a directional consistency filter was applied to identify candidate dysregulations. An LLM-augmented literature screening framework was used to assess the level of literature support for our candidates. Results: Our estimation pipeline showed concordance with reference connectomes, outperformed whole-transcriptome and random-gene co-expression measures, and remained stable when applied to macaque data. A total of 10 connections were marked as candidate dysregulations in schizophrenia at a nominal permutation threshold. Three of the candidates align with established anatomical connectivity, and another three with anatomical connections through relay regions. These candidates were characterized by bidirectional abnormalities in the cortico-striatal circuitry. The remaining four candidates had no well-established monosynaptic connection between two regions. These candidates were interpreted as co-regulated co-expression coordination changes. Literature screening quantified the number of articles discussing each candidate and how many of the articles directly support or refute each candidate. Our candidates collectively highlight the role of the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit in the pathophysiology of schizophrenia. Conclusions: Interregional co-expression of neurotransmission-related genes carries more anatomical information than whole-transcriptome co-expression. Applied to schizophrenia, our analysis recapitulates known hypotheses and also proposes hypothesis-generating data-driven findings for experimental follow-up. This approach complements conventional region-wise analyses. Our approach could support a unified, multi-regional, and multi-neurotransmitter perspective of schizophrenia and point to candidate molecular mechanisms for further studies.

items.title: Human Intestinal Absorption Revisited: The 1998 Descriptors Survive, and the Method Extends to Permeability
items.abstract_or_text: In 1998 we predicted percent human intestinal absorption (HIA) for 86 drug and drug-like compounds from six molecular descriptors chosen by a genetic algorithm with a small neural network serving as the fitness function. That result rested on one division of the compounds into three sets: training, cross-validation and external prediction. Repeating the division shows it was a rather fortunate one. An extraction is one random draw from a wide distribution, so we repeat every experiment 250 times and report the result as a distribution. Across 250 stratified extractions, 14 match the published cross-validation error and only one matches the published external prediction error. Reconstructed this way, the published six descriptors give a mean extraction error roughly twice the external prediction value we reported in 1998 (Table 1). We then applied the same six descriptors to a larger set of 780 compounds from a public compilation. Under the 1998 network they give 22.50 %HIA units on training compounds against 25.77 on extracted compounds, whereas on the 86 they give 13.43 against 30.39. More compounds close the gap between fitting and prediction. Four datasets are modeled here: 780 small molecules with HIA measured in man, 3,771 small molecules and 1,281 cyclic peptides measured across Caco-2 cell monolayers, and 7,298 cyclic peptides measured across artificial membranes. Each is its own prediction problem, and one procedure is applied to all four. A genetic algorithm chooses which descriptors to use and how many, and a random forest grades each choice on compounds its own trees never saw. The descriptors chosen most often across the 250 extractions form one consensus set for each dataset. For absorption, 25 consensus descriptors under a random forest reach an extraction rms of 20.47 %HIA units at R 0.76. On the same compounds and the same extractions, the six 1998 descriptors under the 1998 network reach 25.77 at R 0.59. The four models are served at predicthia.ai, where a structure can be drawn or pasted, scored against its training set for similarity, and the training data with fitted models downloaded. Each model served is its fixed consensus set fitted on every compound in its dataset; the accuracy quoted beside a prediction comes from evaluating that same set across 250 extractions (Table 3). The fixed sets hold 25 descriptors for absorption, 55 for Caco-2 small-molecule permeability, 50 for Caco-2 peptide permeability and 25 for artificial-membrane permeability. Keywords: human intestinal absorption; QSPR; genetic algorithm; descriptor selection; cyclic peptides; membrane permeability; oral bioavailability; repeated extraction

items.title: Concurrent de novo inference of cell types and gene regulatory networks with NetMap
items.abstract_or_text: Existing methods for GRN inference based on single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data typically require prior cell type calling and then infer GRNs at cell type resolution. This risks propagation of errors from cell annotation to GRN inference. Moreover, it makes existing methods blind to regulatory programs that are shared between different cell types, as well as to subtle differences in regulatory activity between cells of the same type. To address these limitations, we present NetMap, a pipeline that jointly infers cell-level GRNs and clusters cells based on shared regulatory programs, combining state-of-the-art single-cell autoencoders and explainable artificial intelligence methods. NetMap outperforms existing methods on synthetic data with a known ground-truth GRN and is able to reliably detect biologically plausible regulons on real data. Moreover, requiring only a small set of user-provided marker genes, NetMap can be used for GRN structure-informed probabilistic cell type assignment. We demonstrate the utility of this approach using PBMC data, where we achieve near perfect clustering and cell type recovery performance compared with manually created cell type labels. Finally, we applied NetMap to a data set with naive, activated and exhausted T-cells, and were able to verify that NetMap retrieves relevant T-cell state signatures from the data, with two approaches. NetMap can be installed as a python package from https://github.com/bionetslab/netmap and is compatible with the scverse system. Scripts to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/bionetslab/netmap-evaluation.

items.title: Cell Painting and machine learning for mechanistic profiling of hepatotoxic botanicals and their constituents
items.abstract_or_text: BACKGROUND Botanicals are widely consumed as herbal remedies and plant-derived products, but their complex and variable chemical composition presents major challenges for safety assessment. Although hepatotoxicity has been reported for several botanicals, the constituent compounds responsible and the underlying mechanisms often remain poorly characterised. OBJECTIVES We aimed to determine whether Cell Painting could identify candidate constituent drivers of botanical bioactivity and generate hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action in primary human hepatocytes. METHODS We profiled 13 botanical extracts and 85 known constituents across multiple concentrations using Cell Painting alongside assays of metabolic activity and membrane integrity. To interpret morphological phenotypes, we trained machine-learning models using a Cell Painting reference atlas of >1,000 chemicals linked to ToxCast/Tox21 molecular and cellular bioactivity annotations. RESULTS Cell Painting detected bioactivity in 11/13 botanical extracts and 46/85 constituents, compared with 9/13 extracts and 40/85 constituents in the cell-health assays, and generally detected activity at lower concentrations. For 9/13 extracts, at least one constituent was active at a lower concentration than the corresponding botanical extract, supporting the contribution of a subset of potent constituents to mixture-level responses. Aristolochia and goldenseal were the most potent extracts across Cell Painting and cell-health assays and contained highly active constituents. Reference-atlas models generated specific mechanistic hypotheses, including cytotoxicity-, endocrine-, and genotoxicity-associated responses for several botanicals and constituents. CONCLUSION These results support Cell Painting combined with machine learning as a sensitive approach for characterising cellular responses to botanicals, prioritising candidate constituent drivers of hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes, and generating testable hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action.

items.title: Prediction of MOF Adsorption Isotherms and High-Throughput Screening Using a Physics-Informed Membranes Graph Neural Network
items.abstract_or_text: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are prime CO 2 -capture candidates, but grand canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) screening is costly when full isotherms, not single uptakes, are required; machine learning surrogates rarely resolve the continuous pressure response. We report a physics-informed pressure-aware multi-task graph neural network (PI-MGNN) to predict CO 2 uptake at arbitrary pressure and reconstruct isotherms from structure. From ~130,000 candidates, PCA and K-means select 5,023 representative MOFs, each simulated by GCMC at five pressures spanning 0.1-5.0 MPa, enforcing a continuous pressure response. Crystal graphs are processed by decoupled geometric and electrostatic graph-attention branches with auxiliary supervision, while a Gaussian-expanded pressure query is fused by cross-attention. PI-MGNN attains R 2 = 0.977 and MAE = 0.291 mol kg -1 ; isotherm MAEs are 0.428/0.312/0.330 mol kg -1 for high/medium/low-uptake MOFs, and cross-attention improves accuracy by 6.3%. Attention weights recover the pressure-resolved physics, enabling accurate and interpretable high-throughput screening.

items.title: UpKast: Method, Model, and Database for Large-Scale Cross-Solvent Determination of pKa Values
items.abstract_or_text: The acid dissociation constant, commonly written as p K a , plays a key role in chemistry. However, most p K a measurements have been conducted in only a handful of solvents, resulting in data scarcity for many relevant solvent systems. Herein, we introduce the UpKast-DB, which comprises of p K a estimates for around 3,000 acids and bases in 29 solvents. We constructed UpKast-DB using a quantum-chemical method that integrates solvation free energy calculations with experimental data. Furthermore, we trained a surrogate machine learning model UpKast-ML on the computed values, allowing for rapid and accurate prediction of p K a values beyond the acids and bases presented in UpKast-DB. The quantum-chemical and machine learning methods result in RMSEs of approximately 1 p K a unit relative to experimental values, slightly higher than the typical aleatoric uncertainty of underlying experimental data, but more accurate than many existing experimental measurements (which can have uncertainties up to, and sometimes beyond, 3 p K a units). The data and modeling approaches provide a means of productively augmenting existing p K a data sources, and represent a significant step toward general determination of p K a in any solvent. The dataset and models can be found on Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23239570

items.title: Zwitterionic Acyl Anion Equivalents from Carboxylic Acids via Acylsulfonylhydrazides: A Practical Organocatalytic Umpolung
items.abstract_or_text: The development of mild and practical acyl anion equivalents remains a cornerstone challenge in modern organic synthesis, as traditional umpolung strategies often rely on moisture-sensitive reagents, strong bases, or specialized N-heterocyclic carbene catalysts. Here we report that readily available N,N-acylsulfonylhydrazides serve as efficient acyl anion surrogates under operationally simple organocatalytic conditions. Using DMAP as a nucleophilic catalyst, these stable hydrazide precursors readily provide acylation products of a wide range of carbon electrophiles, including aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes, activated ketones, olefins, and imines. Mechanistic investigations, supported by DFT calculations and HRMS analysis, reveal an unconventional pathway wherein DMAP adds to the acyldiazene intermediate, triggering nitrogen extrusion and generating a zwitterionic nucleophile. This dual role of DMAP in enhancing both the stability and nucleophilicity of the reactive species circumvents the hydroxycarbene rearrangement pathway, offering a practical and scalable alternative to existing acyl anion methodologies.

items.title: Multivalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly
items.abstract_or_text: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) has emerged as an important intermediate in the pathological self-assembly of Tau, yet the molecular mechanisms that regulate this process remain incompletely understood. Although ubiquitin is a prominent component of pathological inclusions in tauopathies and other neurodegenerative diseases, its presence has largely been linked to targeting aberrant proteins for proteasomal or autophagic clearance. Here, we identify Tau as a ubiquitin-binding protein and demonstrate that multivalent, non-covalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly. Biochemical, biophysical, structural, and computational analyses identified four ubiquitin-binding elements within the Tau microtubule-binding repeat region that engage the canonical hydrophobic patch of ubiquitin, providing a structural basis for multivalent recognition of mono- and poly-ubiquitin species. Functionally, mono- and poly-ubiquitin suppress Tau condensate formation while enhancing the liquid-like properties of condensates that persist. In contrast, mono-ubiquitin selectively enhances aggregation of the disease-linked Tau-P301L variant under conditions without detectable LLPS, demonstrating that ubiquitin exerts distinct effects depending on the molecular context and stage of Tau self-assembly. Together, these findings establish non-covalent ubiquitin recognition as a previously unrecognized mechanism regulating Tau phase behavior and aggregation. More broadly, they expand the role of ubiquitin beyond protein quality control, with ubiquitin architecture providing an additional layer of regulation over Tau condensate formation, dynamics, maturation, and aggregation.

items.title: AI-Driven Design of Next-Generation Immunoinformatics Multi-Epitope Subunit Vaccine Targeting the Most Virulent Mpox Proteome: A Structural and Kinetic Validation Framework
items.abstract_or_text: The resurgence of the Mpox virus (MPXV) highlights the urgent need for scalable, mutation-resistant countermeasures. Slow development timelines hinder traditional empirical vaccine discovery, while conventional vaccinology often yields high false-positive rates because it relies on static, linear sequence-based screening. These classical informatics filters consistently fail to predict physical structural stability or the dynamic presentation of immune cells under physiological conditions, creating a distinct translational gap between computational design and in vitro efficacy. To address these limitations, here we engineered an advanced, AI-augmented vaccine discovery pipeline targeting the most virulent components of the MPXV proteome. We systematically screened eight critical viral targets essential for replication, membrane morphogenesis, and host-cell entry to map highly conserved T-cell and B-cell epitopes. Moving beyond standard heuristic filtering, we implemented a high-fidelity deep learning validation layer: ESM-2 protein language models (pLMs) were deployed to calculate pseudo-perplexity scores across chimeric linker junctions (EAAAK, GPGPG) to guarantee structural naturalness, MHCflurry ensemble models successfully verified active intracellular antigen presentation, and structure-informed graph neural networks (GNNs) simulated the physical node-attention dynamics of the immune synapse. Finally, recurrent neural networks (RNNs)-driven mRNA kinetic modeling optimized translation initiation rates and minimum free energy profiles during in silico cloning. This multi-layered pipeline successfully yielded three structurally refined, multi-epitope vaccine constructs optimized for maximum global population coverage. ESM-2 structural validation confirmed exceptionally low perplexity scores at structural junctions, indicating that the engineered chimaeras have native-like stability and a minimized risk of proteolysis. GNN-based immune synapse modeling demonstrated highly stable binding kinetics and robust binding free energies between the target epitopes and human HLA alleles. Furthermore, RNN kinetic optimizations established that the cDNA sequences are optimized for high-yield expression in heterologous expression hosts without risk of ribosomal stalling or translational bottlenecks. This study establishes a deep learning-augmented framework that bridges the gap between theoretical sequence optimization and biopharmaceutical scalability. By validating the structural naturalness, real-world immunogenicity, and manufacturing kinetics of our vaccine chimeras, this framework presents a robust, proactive paradigm for rapid vaccine architecture against emerging orthopoxvirus threats.

items.title: Microglia transcriptomic response to doxorubicin-induced genotoxic stress
items.abstract_or_text: Chemobrain, characterized by cognitive dysfunction, has emerged as a significant health concern following cancer treatment. Doxorubicin, an FDA-approved chemotherapeutic agent, is widely used to treat various cancers. However, its adverse effects raise concerns regarding toxicity in non-cancerous cell types. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, play a central role in maintaining neural homeostasis. Despite this, the mechanisms by which microglia become dysfunctional following doxorubicin exposure remain poorly understood. Understanding the transcriptomic alterations induced by doxorubicin in microglia could provide critical insights into mechanisms underlying its neurotoxic effects. In this study, the transcriptomic response of human microglia to doxorubicin using mRNA sequencing combined with bioinformatic analysis was investigated. Exposure to doxorubicin significantly altered microglial morphology, promoting a shift toward a process-bearing phenotype in human HMC3 cells. This phenotypic change was accompanied by elevated levels of DNA damage and was associated with the induction of cellular senescence. At the gene regulation level, the Illumina-based transcriptomic analysis provided 25,834 gene expression profiling in which 5,669 were differentially expressed. The future analyses revealed that 3,431 (upregulated) and 2,238 (downregulated) were differentially expressed under the treatment of doxorubicin. Genes associated with the p53 signaling pathway and inflammatory responses were upregulated, whereas genes involved in translation, DNA replication, and cell-cycle progression were downregulated. This transcriptional dysregulation was accompanied by differential expression of key transcription factors. This study provides transcriptomic evidence elucidating the genotoxic response to doxorubicin in microglial cells, offering mechanistic insights into chemobrain and highlighting key molecular pathways as potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

items.title: EvSpark: Lossless Speculative Decoding for Hybrid DNA Foundation Models
items.abstract_or_text: Hybrid DNA foundation models combine convolutional, recurrent, and attention layers, making speculative decoding more difficult than truncating a KV cache. We present EvSpark, a speculative decoding system for Evo2 that verifies draft blocks in parallel and restores all three classes of inference state by selecting retained intermediate states, without replay. A compact, hidden-state-conditioned drafter proposes each block in one parallel forward pass. On Evo2 7B, a 48-prompt benchmark with three training seeds yields a 2.96-fold speedup on 43 real-sequence prompts and a 3.27-fold speedup including five synthetic controls. Acceleration persists at 262k-token context (1.84-2.43-fold speedup on two bacterial genomes) and over 32k generated tokens. Retraining the same drafter architecture for Evo2 20B and 40B yields 2.18-2.46-fold speedups on real sequences and 2.51-2.78-fold speedups on the full suite. Autoregressive drafter comparisons and batch measurements show why low draft latency, rather than acceptance alone, determines the gain. The method preserves the target distribution. Greedy checks find no non-tie divergences across 48 prompts and six checkpoints; complementary sampling diagnostics quantify decoding fidelity. A drafter trained on 30M supervised positions reaches a 2.82-fold speedup on real sequences, compared with a 2.96-fold speedup at 150M positions. In regulatory-DNA design, EvSpark achieves a median 1.57-fold complete-workflow speedup over a calibrated batched native baseline.

items.title: Global statistical constraint and local partner-sensitive inference support dynamic, open-ended verbal coordination
items.abstract_or_text: Effective verbal communication requires individuals to align their communicative intentions through the precise use of utterances, yet how this is achieved in dynamic, open-ended communication remains unclear. Combining predictive deep language models (DLMs) with cognitive computational modeling, we tested a computational division of labor between context-sensitive global constraint on the utterance space and partner-sensitive local adjustment of selection priorities. We formalized local adjustment using an active inference inspired updating rule within a statistical-pragmatic hybrid model. Thirty dyads performed a dynamic, open-ended collaborative word-generation task during functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning. Interlocutors converged in their lexical choices, and lexical alignment was best explained by a hybrid model integrating contextual selection priors with interaction-specific local adjustment among the models tested. This hybrid process formed a dynamic hypothesis landscape comprising a global semantic search region and local selection priorities. Critically, interaction did not simply reduce uncertainty: within individuals, the hypothesis space of global semantic search progressively narrowed while local uncertainty among plausible alternatives increased; between partners, both global hypothesis space and local selection became increasingly aligned, with alignment of local selection priorities most strongly predicting subsequent lexical alignment. The contribution of local adjustment was stronger during precise verbal communication than in the control tasks. Neural analyses further identified correlates of the local adjustment process: temporoparietal and anterior temporal regions supported partner-related inference and semantic prediction error, respectively, and their activity during thinking predicted subsequent inferior frontal activity associated with self-updating during speaking. The participant's own hypothesis landscape was also represented in the left inferior parietal-supramarginal cortex. The main findings generalized across language models and an independent Czech dataset. Together, these findings reveal that alignment in open-ended communication emerges from complementary statistical and pragmatic computations, providing a framework for understanding human and human-AI communication.

items.title: Syntaxin-1 and syntaxin binding protein 1-1 are required for planarian behavior and brain regeneration
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Nervous system regeneration requires creation of new neurons and their integration into new and existing networks. How new neurons find their targets and reconnect in the environment of regenerating tissue remains a major gap in knowledge. The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea is well suited to the study of neural regeneration due to the remarkable ability of planarians to regenerate their entire body, including the nervous system. However, we have not yet been able to explore synaptogenesis in regeneration using planarians due to a lack of tools to study synapses. Here we investigate potential players in planarian synapse, focusing on the conserved syntaxin protein family, which functions in neurotransmitter vesicle fusion at the synapse. Results: We found that reduction of either syntaxin-1 (stx1) or syntaxin-binding protein 1-1 (stxbp1-1) decreased locomotion and impeded brain regeneration, specifically in synapse-rich regions. Conclusions: Our observations support STX-1 and STXBP1-1 as bona fide synapse components, providing a starting point for studies neuronal connectivity during homeostatic remodeling and regeneration.

items.title: Neuropeptide Signaling Promotes Stem-Cell Driven Regeneration in Planarians
items.abstract_or_text: Neurons and neuroendocrine cells produce neuropeptides, which act as long-range signals to modulate organismal state and physiological function. In a few cases, neuropeptides have been thought to promote regeneration, but understanding this connection has been difficult due to the relatively poor regenerative capacity of most traditional model organisms. To test whether neuropeptides drive robust regeneration, we used the highly regenerative asexual planarian flatworm as a model. We began by investigating enzymes that cleave and process pre-propeptides to produce bioactive neuropeptides. We characterized 12 putative neuropeptide-processing enzymes and identified three enzymes, prohormone convertase 2 (pc2), carboxypeptidase E (CPE), and peptidylglycine alpha-hydroxylating monooxygenase (PHM-1) that regulate regeneration through their effects on stem cell differentiation and maintenance. We then investigated 51 of the 52 known neuropeptide-encoding genes in planarians, finding that 16 of these genes promote efficient regeneration and/or stem cell function. Our work indicates that diverse neuropeptides regulate endogenous pluripotent stem cells during homeostasis and in robust regeneration. Our data supports a key role for neuropeptide signaling in planarians to promote a pro-regenerative state, which could be valuable to mimic in regenerative therapies.

items.title: Representing biological concepts as directions in foundation model embeddings
items.abstract_or_text: Biological foundation models encode rich information about protein structure, function, and cellular state in high-dimensional embeddings, but accessing specific biological properties typically relies on additional, task-specific prediction models. Here, we show that diverse biological properties can be mapped to interpretable, reusable directions in embedding space. In the Concept Activation Vector (CAV) approach, examples representing a concept are distinguished from a background set using a linear model, and the resulting weight vector defines the CAV for that concept. In protein embeddings, CAVs recover Gene Ontology and Enzyme Commission annotations, localize Pfam domains, reveal novel structural relationships, and capture DNA-binding and protein-interaction interface specificity. In single-cell embeddings, CAVs isolate cancer-associated expression transitions, and gene variation along these axes substantially agrees with conventional differential-expression analysis despite being a distinct computational approach. Together, these results establish concept directions as a common representation, enabling diverse biological features to be compared, localized, and manipulated.

items.title: From APTs to advanced persistent biological threats (APBTs): a taxonomy and large-scale metadata audit of genomic surveillance infrastructure
items.abstract_or_text: Open genomic repositories have become critical infrastructure for pathogen surveillance, variant tracking, outbreak reconstruction, and public health decision making. However, many of these repositories were designed to support rapid scientific data sharing rather than adversarial verification, creating potential security gaps. This paper introduces Advanced Persistent Biological Threats (APBTs), as a framework for understanding how malicious cyber biological actors can gradually disrupt genomic surveillance without entering a laboratory or releasing a biological agent. Instead of altering biological material, an attacker targets the sequence data, metadata, reference datasets, and analytical models used by surveillance systems. We present, to our knowledge, the first integrated multilayer taxonomy of APBTs, structured around a four phase lifecycle, and investigate whether the metadata weaknesses identified by this framework are present in an operational genomic repository. To assess this, we audited 100,000 SARS-CoV-2 BioSample records obtained from the NCBI. A framework of 23 checks was applied across five metadata layers: temporal, geographic, host and specimen, provenance, and technical metadata. Every record triggered at least one APBT relevant metadata vulnerability indicator, with a mean of 7.34 indicators per record (SD = 1.34). Overall, 97.3% of records were classified in the High or Critical severity categories. Every record also contained at least one indicator in both the provenance and technical metadata layers. These results largely reflect the optional status of several fields in the current BioSample submission model rather than isolated errors by individual data contributors. Temporal and geographic information was comparatively complete, while fields needed for provenance reconstruction, chain of custody assessment, technical validation, and analytical interpretation were frequently missing. These findings do not indicate deliberate manipulation.
