However, the structural incompleteness of BioSample metadata creates vulnerabilities that an adversary can exploit to introduce poisoned, misleading, or weakly traceable metadata into genomic repositories. As a result, maliciously altered metadata can appear plausible, remain undetected, and influence downstream genomic analysis and surveillance. The findings therefore show that widely used pathogen genomic repositories already contain structural weaknesses that can support metadata poisoning as part of an APBT operation.

items.title: Neural prediction decorrelation reveals that adversarial robustness substantially improves DNN prediction accuracy across the entire human auditory cortex
items.abstract_or_text: Sensory neuroscientists seek to model the neural computations that encode complex stimuli. Distinct encoding models often make similar predictions for natural stimuli such as speech, posing a challenge for model comparison. We developed a method to synthesize stimuli that decorrelate model predictions across a neural population, termed neural prediction decorrelation (NPD). Using fMRI responses to NPD sounds, we compared standard and adversarially robust deep neural network models of human auditory cortex. Prediction accuracy for NPD sounds was substantially better for the adversarially robust model in every region tested, an effect completely masked with natural sounds. Population responses to natural and synthesized NPD sounds shared an interpretable low-dimensional organization that was reproduced by the robust encoding model. NPD provides a general approach for comparing encoding models and reveals that adversarial robustness expands the predictive power of DNNs beyond natural stimuli, which is likely critical for targeting population activity through stimulus synthesis.

items.title: Understanding when and how knowledge graphs add value to EHR-based clinical prediction across Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, and chronic pain
items.abstract_or_text: Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as a promising approach for incorporating biological knowledge into machine-learning models trained on electronic health record (EHR) data. However, their large scale and heterogeneous structure impose substantial computational cost, and it remains unclear whether their benefits generalize across diseases or depend on how the graph is constructed. We systematically evaluated KG integration across three diseases spanning distinct biological and clinical characteristics: multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, and chronic pain. For each disease we compared five modelling strategies, spanning EHR-only features and graph diffusion over concept-level, cohort-derived, disease-anchored, and full SPOKE (Scalable Precision Medicine Open Knowledge Engine) subgraphs, asking whether graph construction affects predictive performance and computational cost, whether KG integration improves classification over EHR-only models, and what the graph does to model behavior. Cohort-derived subgraphs, comprising roughly 45% of SPOKE's nodes and one-fifth of its edges, matched or modestly exceeded the full graph's performance while substantially reducing computational cost in all three diseases. The predictive benefit of KG integration, however, was strongly disease-dependent: it improved classification in Parkinson's disease, had no measurable effect in multiple sclerosis, and reduced performance in chronic pain. These differences were not explained by the amount of biological information incorporated: the disease with the largest shift toward molecular features showed no improvement, the sole beneficiary showed only a modest shift, and the disease with no molecular shift was penalized. Mechanistically, graph diffusion redistributed each disease's existing signal across many correlated features rather than adding independent biological signal, so that any gain depended on whether it added information beyond the EHR. These findings show that cohort-derived subgraphs offer a computationally efficient alternative to full-scale knowledge graphs, and that KG integration functions less as a universal accuracy booster than as a data- and disease-dependent transformation of the patient representation.

items.title: CodonBench: separating gene context, exon position, and variant-specific component in synonymous-variant classification
items.abstract_or_text: Background. A synonymous variant leaves the protein unchanged, so a classifier that still separates pathogenic from benign examples must be reading something beyond the protein. Such variants test cleanly what a codon-level model adds to a protein-level one. Methods. We assembled SynPath, a benchmark of ClinVar synonymous variants, and scored frozen representations under two splitting protocols. Under gene-held-out folds whole genes are withheld, and each coding-sequence model is compared against a position-matched control. Results. The models were not trained for this task, so these numbers describe transfer, not designed performance. Random splitting flatters every representation. Once whole genes are held out, they fall into a narrow band near chance, the best at 0.58, and low-rank fine-tuning does not restore the random-split level. A feature that reads no sequence, only the distance from the variant to the nearest exon junction, reaches 0.84 under the same folds, above every neural representation tested. In a protein model the variant-specific component is zero by construction, because both alleles present the same input. In coding-sequence models only the response vector, the difference between the alternate and reference embeddings, keeps signal on unseen genes and beats its position-matched control. Conclusions. Synonymous-variant pathogenicity is predictable mainly from gene identity and from position. Only a small part reflects the variant itself, and only in models that read the coding sequence. Benchmarks judged on random splits will overstate what these models have learned.

items.title: Astrocytes in the Dentate Gyrus Shift the Equilibrium from Pattern Separation to Pattern Completion and Inhibit Fear Extinction
items.abstract_or_text: Pattern separation and pattern completion are core hippocampal computations linked to memory interference and overgeneralization in many neuropsychiatric disorders and to mnemonic discrimination deficits in neurodegenerative conditions. Astrocytes are increasingly recognized as important integrators and modulators of neuronal activity as many studies have shown changes in animal behavior and neural circuits induced by manipulation of astrocytic activity. The role of astrocytes in the dentate gyrus for learning and memory is, however, largely unknown. To investigate the functional significance of astrocytic activity in the dentate gyrus, we expressed the calcium extruding pump hPMCA2w/b (CalEx), resulting in inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity, the Gq-coupled receptor hM3Dq, or the Gi-coupled receptor hM4Di, allowing chronic activation of Gq- and Gi-dependent pathways by a designer drug, in dentate gyrus astrocytes. Our main finding is that inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity by CalEx resulted in improved pattern separation and impaired pattern completion. In -vivo calcium imaging revealed that CalEx expression in astrocytes altered the neuronal activity pattern in dentate gyrus neurons with an overall inhibitory effect. This suggests that in the dentate gyrus astrocytes promote the activity of these neurons. Furthermore, chronic activation of hM4Di resulted in impaired between-session fear extinction while chronic activation of hM3Dq resulted in impaired within-session fear extinction and improved pattern separation learning over multiple days, suggesting that activation of astrocytic activity enhances mechanistically separable forms of fear extinction in a Gq- or Gi-pathway-specific manner. Our findings reveal that dentate gyrus astrocytic calcium shifts the balance between pattern separation and pattern completion towards pattern completion and thus modulates an essential neuronal functional output of the dentate gyrus. Chronic activation of astrocytes inhibits fear extinction, and thus also affects management of memory interference. Our findings imply that astrocytic modulation may be beneficial to treat cognitive deficits in disorders in which overgeneralization is a problem.

items.title: Developmental rewiring of EHMT1 function during human cortical neurogenesis
items.abstract_or_text: Ubiquitously expressed chromatin regulators orchestrate cell-type-specific gene expression programs, yet how they acquire distinct regulatory functions during development remains fundamentally unresolved. Using temporally controlled protein depletion during human cortical neurogenesis in vitro, we show that the autism-associated histone methyltransferase EHMT1 is developmentally repurposed from epiblast to cortical neurons. Broadly expressed zinc finger proteins recruit EHMT1 to distinct cis-regulatory elements within changing chromatin landscapes associated with lineage-specific transcription factor activity, with extensive remodeling of EHMT1 enhancer occupancy during neural induction dependent on ZNF462. This genomic rewiring is accompanied by a fundamental shift from restraining premature developmental gene expression in pluripotent cells to supporting neuronal programs, with distinct transcriptional consequences of EHMT1 loss across neural progenitors and excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes. Timed depletion and recovery experiments identify the neural progenitor stage as the onset of a developmental period during which EHMT1 is required for faithful neuronal maturation. Remarkably, EHMT1 can re-engage stage-specific targets after prolonged deficiency, allowing extensive transcriptional recovery with only limited molecular scarring. These findings reveal how ubiquitous epigenetic machinery acquires developmental specificity while demonstrating the resilience of developmental gene regulatory programs to prolonged disruption, with implications for neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: Subtype-Selective Neuronal Vulnerability and Compensatory Neuroglial Remodeling in Human Cortical Dementia
items.abstract_or_text: Whether the nodal vulnerability in dementia is solely represented by changes in cellular abundance or attrition of cellular transcriptomic landscape attribute to that transition in aging brain is yet to uncover with minutiae. To understand this complication, we have analyzed two snRNA-seq data specific to (I) dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC): A comprehensive study of cellular profiling among cognitively normal and pathological ageing and dementia (AD) brain, (II) occipital cortex (OC) in the context of Nasu-Hakola disease along with a tissue level bulk RNA-seq data corresponds to temporal cortex. We pinpoint cellular subpopulations their proportional changes within the nodal points and their transcriptomic profiling. In DLPFC we observed alteration of mitochondrial and synaptic maintenance program in the pathological manifestation of disease. In OC we noticed depleted upper layer CUX2 neuron, PVALB and SST neurons on the contrary an enrichment of RORB and LAMP5 neurons with compromised metabolic states in the disease context. Glial populations are marked by representation of fibrous astrocyte, neuronal-supporting subpopulations associated with extracellular matrix remodeling programs. Proportional increment of intermediate myelinating oligodendrocyte and a decrease in mature myelinating subpopulation highlighted a compromised myelin repair attempt. In temporal cortex at tissue level we observed transcriptomic landscape adopted a neuroglial phenotypes in dementia brain. Cell-Chat analysis demonstrated a shift in cellular coordination towards glial population from neuron in NHD brain. A single cell-based drug reprofiling approach identified efatutazone and balaglitazone as broad-spectrum candidates for major cell types in occipital cortex, whereas major actionable biological targets belong to CDK subtypes and proteasome subunits. Overall, our findings imply cellular persistence do not necessarily substantiate molecular preservation, also the coexistence of cellular vulnerability alongside selective remodeling features, present a cellular framework on how to cope up with degenerative changes.

items.title: Unraveling phenotypic variation in multiscale behavioral dynamics
items.abstract_or_text: Behavioral variability reflects differences in internal and external parameters and provides a substrate for natural selection. However, uncovering its structure is challenging because behavior evolves nonlinearly across multiple timescales. Our goal is to reconstruct phenotypic variation from finite behavioral observations without prescribing the scales at which individuals should be compared. To achieve this, we introduce a multiscale dissimilarity that compares dynamics across all statistically resolvable resolutions by constructing reduced transfer operators at progressively finer scales and weighting their differences by finite-sampling uncertainty. This dissimilarity defines a geometry of dynamical phenotypes, which we reconstruct using diffusion maps. We show that the resulting phenotypic coordinates locally follow the parameter directions to which dynamics are most sensitive. We validate our approach in a stochastic model and apply it to bacterial and larval zebrafish behavior. In bacteria, we identify run speed as a major component of inter-individual variability, associated with the chemotaxis protein CheB. In zebrafish, we find that prior prey experience reshapes behavioral dynamics and phenotypic variability, with paramecia experience concentrating fish in a prey-capture-associated region of phenotypic space. Together, these results provide a framework for identifying internal and environmental variables that structure dynamical phenotypes across scales.

items.title: Gold nanofibers as scaffolds for neuron differentiation in a 3D microtissue
items.abstract_or_text: Engineering neuronal tissues requires biomaterials that provide structural support while actively directing cell fate. Here, high-aspect-ratio gold nanofibers are explored as bioinstructive scaffolds for neuronal organization and differentiation. In a 2.5D paper-based model, the nanofibers guide Neuro-2a cell organization and promote neurite-like extensions through topographical interactions. Building on these findings, a printable composite bioink comprising a gelatin/alginate liquid phase and gelatin microstrands is fabricated. The resulting inks exhibit shear-thinning behavior, rapid structural recovery, and sufficient mechanical stability for extrusion-based 3D bioprinting. Incorporation of SH-SY5Y cells generates viable and proliferative progenitor microtissues, with increasing gelatin microstrand content favoring neuronal-like morphologies. Integration of the gold nanofibers further enhances neuronal differentiation, as supported by cell morphology, immunostaining, and expression of neuronal markers, with differentiation occurring even in the absence of retinoic acid, a common chemical differentiation factor. Spatial separation of the gold nanofibers from the cells reduces this effect, highlighting the importance of direct cell-material interactions. Together, these results establish high-aspect-ratio gold nanofibers provide structural cues capable of promoting neuronal differentiation within 3D bioprinted tissues and provide a strategy for engineering neuron-like microtissues without relying exclusively on chemical differentiation agents.

items.title: Transformation product bottleneck: Photo-recalcitrance of rotenolone limits the aquatic degradation of rotenone in a temperature-dependent manner
items.abstract_or_text: The environmental fate and toxicity of transformation products (TPs) are frequently overlooked. However, in many cases, TPs are functional analogs that exhibit similar, and often greater, toxicity as the parent compound. In cases where the TP is persistent in the environment, the rate of TP degradation can influence the overall environmental fate. Rotenolone (12𝛼-hydroxy-rotenone, ROH) is the primary TP of rotenone (ROT), a pesticide utilized ubiquitously and highly popular in cold regions. Both ROT and ROH are mitochondrial NADH inhibitors, however ROH is more persistent than ROT and remains unregulated. 2 This work investigated the aquatic photochemical pathways and transformation products of ROH, including simulated Subarctic (low-temperature) conditions. Given that ROT degradation is driven by photolysis, we hypothesized that inhibited photochemical activity of ROH accounts for its persistence. Our results suggest ROH persistence is largely attributed to significantly reduced triplet state lifetimes, absorbance, and apparent quantum yields. Temperature was identified as a significant driver of ROH photolysis, accelerating the direct photochemical transformation rate, with half-lives ranging from approximately 115 h (6 °C) to 66 h (19 °C). This suggests that the cool temperatures of Subarctic surface waters further contribute to ROH persistence. Degradation was accelerated in the presence of chromophoric dissolved organic matter (CDOM); Fenton experiments confirmed ROH reacts with hydroxyl radical at near diffusion-limited rates (2.9×1010 ± 1.1×109 M-1 s-1 at 20 °C). Nontarget analysis of ROH photoproducts revealed novel transformation intermediates not previously identified. These were observed to further transform to smaller products, suggesting that ROH photochemical transformation represents the final step in detoxification. Thus, the photochemical recalcitrance of ROH is involved in limiting the detoxification of ROT following aquatic pesticidal use. These results strongly suggest including ROH monitoring during ROT pesticide applications.

items.title: Insights Into an Antibacterial Type VI Membrane-Disrupting Effector Of Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli
items.abstract_or_text: Adherent Invasive Escherichia coli (AIEC) strains are associated with ileal Crohn's disease and may contribute to intestinal dysbiosis through antibacterial competition. The AIEC reference strain LF82 encodes two type VI secretion systems (T6SSs), a contractile machine that injects an effector-loaded needle made of Hcp, VgrG and PAAR into neighbouring rivals, favoring niche colonization. LF82 T6SSs harbour several putative antibacterial toxin-immunity modules. Here we characterize the T6SS-1 encoded TmeAIEC, a PAAR-fused T6SS effector carrying a C-terminal Tme domain, hallmark of Tme (Type VI membrane disrupting effector) toxins, and its DUF1240-like immunity protein TmiAIEC. When heterologously produced in E. coli K-12 as well as in E. coli and Citrobacter clinical isolates, TmeAIEC is toxic only upon periplasmic targeting, and its toxicity is neutralized by TmiAIEC. Periplasmically-targeted TmeAIEC inserts into the inner membrane, collapses the proton motive force and increases cell permeability, consistent with a membrane-disrupting activity. Mutational analyses coupled to functional assays identified a predicted hydrophobic transmembrane segment and a conserved aspartate residue within the Tme domain as key determinants for TmeAIEC toxicity. These findings establish TmeAIEC/TmiAIEC as a functional T6SS toxin-immunity pair and reveal conserved determinants underlying the activity of Tme-family membrane-disrupting effectors.

items.title: Tracking Without Linking or Localization: Single-Photon Tracking
items.abstract_or_text: Mobile biological particles, ranging from biomolecules to viral capsids, often diffuse faster than 1m2/s, resulting in severe motion blur in conventional millisecond-scale imaging. Shorter exposures capture faster dynamics, but quantizing the per-pixel signal at such exposures eventually degrades our ability to localize particles at all. In the extreme case of binary (1-bit-per-pixel) output--where moving from 8-bit grayscale to 1-bit corresponds to a 255-fold faster acquisition rate--no existing tracking method applies, since all of them rely on intensity-based localization that binary data cannot supply. We therefore introduce single-photon single-particle tracking (SP2T), a framework that bypasses localization and linking by estimating particle numbers and trajectories directly from the full 1-bit image stack. We demonstrate SP2T on single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) arrays, which deliver microsecond exposures over a large field of view (512x512 pixels) and explicitly account for detector-specific artifacts such as hot and cold pixels. We validate the method against programmed fluorescent bead and organic dye trajectories, and apply it to two biological systems, aerolysin and ganglioside GM1. Together with simulation, these experiments reveal that longer exposures bias diffusion coefficient estimates (by up to 70% for particles diffusing at 5m2/s) and distort jump-distance distributions, underscoring the need for photon-by-photon tracking in fast-diffusion regimes. Evaluating the likelihood on a GPU further delivers more than a 50-fold speedup over a CPU implementation when compared on datasets of the same frame size and number of frames, enabling multiplexed tracking for crowded particles. Together, these advances establish SP2T as a robust, data-efficient route to unbiased particle tracking at microsecond temporal resolution.

items.title: Beyond Ramachandran distributions: quantifying secondary structure effects on amino acids and their pairs in the full torsional space
items.abstract_or_text: The Ramachandran diagram has long served for understanding protein secondary structure elements (SSEs), despite the multitude of factors contributing to their occurrence. Starting from recentlyintroduced circula-based multivariate torsion-angle distribution (CBMD) mixture models -- accommodating covariance structure in the full torsion-angle space of amino acids, we define continuous densities for the 20 amino acids and 400 amino-acid pairs in dimension up to 14, conditioned by SSE labels. Projecting these higher-dimensional distributions onto the classical Ramachandran diagram reveals how secondary structures in the protein universe emerge from amino-acid-dependent conformational preferences reflecting influences beyond backbone dihedrals alone. Our analysis links the traditional geometric description of local protein structure to modern statistical models of the full conformational space of amino acids and amino-acidpairs, while providing a framework for generating protein conformations consistent with any given secondary structure environment -- a feature that remains difficult to enforce explicitly in current AI-based generative models.

items.title: Unsupervised decomposition of massively parallel TraDIS-Xpress fitness data from Escherichia coli identifies distinct functional and expression modules of antimicrobial resistance determinants
items.abstract_or_text: Linking genotype to phenotype is a central goal in biology, one way to do this is using transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) where the fitness impacts of mutations across a genome are assessed in different conditions. Traditional analyses use comparison of each gene response independently in control versus test conditions, so a compendium of hundreds of test conditions returns hundreds of separate ranked gene lists. To unlock the potential information hidden within large data sets, we applied independent component (ICA) analysis to 754 Escherichia coli BW25113 TraDIS-Xpress samples. These samples included a series of antibiotic and other stress condition exposures. ICA is designed to identify hidden structure within complex data and to extract meaningfully linked components. In this analysis each annotated gene was resolved into a gene body and 198 bp 5' and 3' features so that expression effects driven by the transposon's outwards facing promoter enter the matrix separately from gene disruption effects. The decomposition returned 99 components, which we term fxModules, which were defined as containing elements with similar responses across the whole compendium rather than per any individual experiment. Of the 754 stress samples, the antibiotic arm included 110 samples derived from exposure to 14 separate agents at multiple concentrations. Many of these have been highly studied allowing us to explore the accuracy of predicted responsive fxModules. This analysis showed excellent predictive power of the approach and the fxModules responsive to individual drugs typically reproduced known mechanisms at a resolution superior to analysis of single gene sets. For example, exposure to fosfomycin identified responsive fxModules containing genes which are known to be involved in uptake of the drug, cAMP-CRP control and exposure to gentamicin identified oxidative phosphorylation split across three fxModules responding with different magnitudes and directions at different concentrations. This recapitulates recent work studying the landscape of E. coli genes sensitive to this drug with high precision without any prior knowledge of functional annotation. Similarly precise predictions were made for other drugs. Responsive modules also identified novel groups of genes and linkages beyond the boundaries of defined pathways as being responsive to various stresses demonstrating the ability to predict new genotype-phenotype links. Inclusion of the regulatory regions also resolved fxModules which were entirely contributed by promoter regions, for example for chloramphenicol genes responsible for efflux were identified by signals in intergenic control regions, and unidirectional insertions in gene bodies, a signal that a gene level matrix would not be able to predict with accuracy. These data show that ICA decomposition provides an efficient and accurate annotation independent approach to identifying sets of genes with related functional impacts in any given condition in the compendium. The functional modular association of genes also help in predicting gene functions of unknown genes based on the group function. This approach allows rapid identification of novel genotype-phenotype links and unlocks the power of multiple comparisons of transposon mutagenesis data.

items.title: Intracellular accumulation of AAV6 genomes governs microglia reactivity and the inflammatory response in retinal gene therapy
items.abstract_or_text: Adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors possess immense potential for gene therapy applications. However, microglia can mount an immune response against AAV vectors. Yet, microglia are therapeutic targets since they play a driving role in the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. Thus, it is critical to understand the cellular processes driving the microglia-mediated immune response against AAV vectors. To this end, we modelled AAV6 induced inflammation upon retinal gene therapy in minipigs. Upon AAV6 administration, the IBA1+ cells demonstrated a morphological transition to the amoeboid form, indicating microglial reactivity. We also observed the invasion of peripheral immune cells in the retina. To elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms, we transduced human iPSC derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs) in vitro with AAV6 and AAV8 respectively. Only AAV6 transduced iMGLs exhibited morphological features and a transcriptomic signature of microglial reactivity. The magnitude of intracellular AAV6 viral genomes was significantly higher as compared to the AAV8 condition. The elevated levels of intracellular AAV6 genomes induced a DNA damage response in AAV6-transduced iMGLs, which is a key feature of neuroinflammation-linked microglial reactivity. Thus, our work highlights the impact of intracellular viral genome accumulation on microglial reactivity and its implications for retinal gene therapy associated inflammation.

items.title: FMR1 Perturbations Disrupt Sensory Corticostriatal Circuits and Mitochondrial Energetics in Fragile X Syndrome
items.abstract_or_text: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) features sensory, social, and cognitive dysfunction, but how fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) deficiency disrupts sensory corticostriatal circuitry and whether distinct FMR1 perturbations converge on shared cellular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. We integrated diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in individuals with FXS and Fmr1-knockout (KO) mice with projection-defined calcium recording, bidirectional optogenetic manipulation, primary somatosensory cortex (S1)-targeted expression of three patient-associated FMR1 missense variants, regional transcriptomics, and optical manipulation of mitochondrial energetic state. Individuals with FXS exhibited disrupted sensory corticostriatal structural connectivity, with mouse analyses further localizing abnormalities to S1-striatal pathways. Fmr1 deficiency impaired recruitment of the S1-dorsomedial striatum (DMS) pathway during social interaction, and projection-specific manipulation demonstrated that S1-DMS dysfunction contributes to social and cognitive deficits. Three patient-associated FMR1 variants, I234T, E329G, and R586Q, converged on social behavioral deficits, which were improved by S1-DMS activation. Transcriptomic analyses revealed convergent oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-related mitochondrial remodeling in S1 and DMS across Fmr1 deficiency and variant models. Systemic treatment with the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ attenuated novel-location-recognition, social-interaction, and social-novelty deficits in Fmr1-KO mice. Moreover, mt-EcGAPR-based Mitochondrial OptoEnergetic Activation (Mito-OptoEA) enhanced mitochondrial energetic state in S1 and improved novel-location recognition and sociability in both Fmr1-KO and I234T models. Together, these findings define a sensory corticostriatal circuit-metabolic framework for FXS in which S1-DMS circuit dysfunction and convergent mitochondrial energetic abnormalities contribute to FMR1-related social and cognitive phenotypes.
